 **A Deep Dive into the MARES software**

We have the classical C++ file setup: 

1) **Header files**: these contain the class definitions together with variables and member functions.  
     
2) **Source files**: these contain the implementation or definition of the different member functions.  
     
3) **Executables**: these are the actual files we want to run after compiling the MARES project.

In this document we describe the different classes in MARES with the goal of upgrading the software step by step in the most efficient way. We already described future potential upgrades in the different git branches of the project ([https://github.com/radarEchoTelescope/MARES](https://github.com/radarEchoTelescope/MARES)) . This document will be kept up to date with what is implemented in the *development branch.* 

The MARES code is built using as many safety nets to prevent accidentally overriding important variables like for example the transmit frequency of the antennas or the primary energy of the neutrino. This is realised by making as many parameters of a class *private* or *protected*. Still, when running the code, these parameters have to be accessible by instances of a different class. In order to access them risk-free, multiple public member functions have been defined that simply return the value of the parameter. We call these member functions, *accessors*. This document will describe the different classes and their member functions and variables. For each class, we start off with describing its general objective. We continue by describing its variables through listing and explaining the different accessors. Next, we describe the constructor of the class; the function that is called when creating a new instance (called object) of that class. We end with describing all the (non-accessor) member functions.

**Part 1: Antennas and Detectors**  
This section will cover the implementation of the antennas in MARES. The code allows for having multiple transmitter antennas and receiver antennas. It is important to note that both types of antennas are instances of the same ***Antenna*** class. They are distinguished from one another in the code by the chosen power of the antenna. A receiver antenna has by definition zero power, a transmitter non-zero power. The declaration and definitions of the Antenna class can be found in antenna.hh and antenna.cc.   
The combination of all transmitters and receivers makes up a complete detector setup. MARES has a dedicated ***Detector*** class that groups all the antenna objects to form a detector and work with easily in the code. The Detector class is a *friend* of the Antenna class. This implies instances of Detector can access all the private variables of Antenna that are declared and defined in respectively the antenna.hh and antenna.cc file together with their member functions and variables. 

1) **Antenna class**

The accessors: 

* double Freq(): returns fFrequency,  the frequency of the antenna in *Hz* (set in cfg).  
* double Wavelength(): returns fWavelength, the wavelength of the antenna in *m.*  
* double Wavenumber(): returns fWavenumber, the wavenumber (2\*pi \*frequency/c\_ice) of the antenna in *m\-1.*  
* double AngularFreq(): returns fAngularFreq, the angular frequency (2\*pi \*frequency) of the antenna *Hz\-1.*  
* double Power(): returns fPower, the power of the antenna in *W* (set in cfg).  
* double Gain(): returns fGain, the gain of the antenna in *dBi* (set in cfg).  
* double E0(): returns k\*(Z\*P/G) .  
* double Leff(): returns fLeff, the effective length of the antenna in *mm*, default 1 m.   
* double Load(): returns fLoad, the antenna load in *Ohm*, default 50 Ohm.   
* double Efficiency(): returns fEff, the antenna efficiency. This parameter determines the losses due to reflections in the cables and more. The default is set to 1 (perfect antenna).  
* double Dot(): returns fDot, the cos(TVP or RVP) if you have TX or RX antenna.   
* double Delta(): returns fDelta, the TVP or RVP angle in *rad*.  
* double Dist(): returns fDistance, the distance between antenna and cascade vertex in *m*.  
* std::vector\<double\> Pos(): returns fPosition, the position vector of the antenna in cartesian coordinates in *m*.  
* std::vector\<double\> Pol(): returns fPolarization, the polarisation vector of the antenna.   
* std::vector\<double\> Dir(): returns fDirection, the direction vector between the antenna and the cascade in *m*. Depending on the type of antenna (transmitter or receiver) this vector is calculated differently. It is calculated according to the way the ray would travel: TX-\>CS-\>RX. This convention only dictates the direction of the vector, not its length.  
* std::vector\<double\> Sph(): returns fSphericalAngles, a vector with the zenith angle and azimuth angle of the direction vectors defined in Dir() in *rad*. 


  We notice that all the variable names have an f character in front of them, e.g. fPower or fFrequency. This naming  convention says that the Antenna class has a friend class Detector. 


  The constructor: 

  Antenna(double xpos, double ypos, double zpos,  double xpol, double ypol, double zpol, double power, double frequency, double gaindB): 

  This is the constructor of the antenna class. It requires you to give as input parameters the position of the antenna, its polarisation, power, frequency and gain. When calling this constructor it immediately links the input values to the corresponding member variables. Hence it sets: fPower, fFrequency, fWavelength, fAngularFreq, fWavenumber, fGain, fPosition, fPolarization. It also calculates the fLeff upon initialisation.


  The member functions that calculate the above quantities depending on antenna position and cascade vertex: 

* void SetDirection(std::vector\<double\> coords): This function calculates the fDirection vector, fDistance and fSphericalAngles doubles w.r.t. the coords vector input variable, which is a scatter point of the cascade (see ScatterPoint structure).   
* void SetAngle(std::vector\<double\> dir): This function calculates the fDot and fDelta variables (see Delta() and Dot() for explanation).    
* double GainDipole(double theta): This function calculates the gain of the antenna in a certain direction *theta*. The standard Gain pattern in MARES is that of a modified Hertzian Dipole: fGain \* sin(theta)^2.6. fGain=pow(10., gaindB/10.) where gaindB is the value set in the config file. fGain is the gain in the direction of maximal directivity. 


2) **Detector class**

the default constructor is empty. A second constructor exists with input variable the name of a default detector setup. There is a StarGrid layout hardcoded in the antenna header file. These are made using a namespace. Usually, the user includes the detector setup via the cfg file. 

The accessors:

* std::vector\<Antenna\> Transmitters(): This is a function that returns the fTransmitters vector.   
  * std::vector\<Antenna\> fTransmitters: A vector containing all the transmitters. Hence, each element is an instance of the antenna class.  
* std::vector\<Antenna\> Receivers(): This is a function that returns the fReceivers vector.   
  * std::vector\<Antenna\> fReceivers: A vector containing all the receivers. Hence, each element is an instance of the antenna class.

	The constructor:

* Detector(): this constructor does not require any input variables. It simply makes an instance of the class in the memory.   
* Detector(std::string name): this constructor requires the name of the detector. There are three hardcoded detector setups in MARES: “bistatic”, “T576”, “Stargrid”. When calling this constructor, the antenna objects are immediately initialised and added to the transmitter and receiver lists of the Detector object. It is advised to not use this constructor and define the detector setup using config files. It corresponds with older code. 

	  
	The member functions: 

* void add\_antenna(Antenna& at): This member function adds the input variable to the correct antenna array. If the fPower is non-zero the antenna is considered to be a transmitter, otherwise a receiver.   
* void add\_antenna(Antenna at): This member function adds the input variable to the correct antenna array. If the fPower is non-zero the antenna is considered to be a transmitter, otherwise a receiver.   
    
  There are also three functions defined that allow to load antennas and detector setups from a config file. We can also load a detector from a separate detector file. These are not member functions of the Antenna or Detector class but are “helper functions” to create instances of those classes. Hence, they are located in the antenna.hh and antenna.cc file. Three functions are responsible for this:   
* void load\_antenna\_list(libconfig::Setting& at\_list,Detector& dect): This function looks at the antenna list in your config file, creates an antenna object for each antenna and adds it to the antenna list of the input detector object.  
* Detector load\_detector\_config(libconfig::Config& dect\_config): This function loads the complete detector in MARES, based on the input of the config file. It uses the above load\_antenna\_list() to add all the receivers and transmitters to the simulation.  
* Detector load\_detector\_file(const std::string& dect\_config\_filepath): This function loads the detector in MARES given the filepath to the config file. (not used).


  
**Part 2: The particle cascade**  
This part will cover the implementation of the particle cascade in MARES. It consists of a single class called **Cascade.** The declaration and definition of the class and all its member functions and variables can be found in the cascade.hh and cascade.cc files. An important remark to make is the fact that this class uses a lot of *overloaded functions*. These functions have the same name but a different implementation, input variables and/or return type. These functions will be indicated in blue for extra clarity. 

The accessors: 

* int Evt() const: returns fEvent, the event number or primary identifier (dummy, I believe this should return n\_num from below).  
* int Nprimaries() const: returns fNp, the number of primaries (dummy, not implemented).  
* double Energy() const: returns fEnergy, the primary energy of the cascade in *GeV*.    
* double Xtot() const: returns fXtot.This corresponds with length of the cascade as a function of column depth X in *g/cm^2*: fXtot \= Ltot\_factor \* log(12.72 \* fEnergy) \* X\_0. The factor for this length can be set in the config file, but the default value is 3 (see settings\_defaults.cc). This is sufficient to catch the full cascade in the longitudinal dimension.   
* double Ltot() const: returns fLtot. This parameter corresponds with the considered longitudinal dimension of the simulated cascade in *cm*: fLtot \= fXtot/rho\_ice (see Xtot() for more info).   
* double Rtot() const: returns fRtot. This parameter corresponds with the radial dimension of the cascade in *cm*. This is expressed in factors of the moliere radius: fRtot \= Rtot\_factor \* r\_moliere. Once again, the factor can be set in the config file. The default value is 2 (see settings\_defaults.cc). This is sufficient to catch the full cascade in the radial dimension. r\_moliere in ice is  7 cm. 		  
* std::vector\<double\> Dir() const: returns fDirection, the cascade direction as a vector in (unit vector) *m.*  
* std::vector\<double\> Pos() const: returns fPosition, the cascade position vector in *m*.  
* std::vector\<double\> Sph() const: returns fSphericalAngles, the cascade direction vector (zenith, azimuth) in *deg*.  
* int\* Info(): returns fParent. This is a vector parameter with as elements: fParent{n\_num,t\_num,p\_id,i\_type,channel}. ⇒ not implemented correctly or used anywhere. See constructor meaning n\_num,... .   
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Ne(): returns fNe, the 2D electron density array. It stores the e\-/cm3 as a function of the longitudinal and lateral dimension of the cascade (L,r). This function is used to save the profile in a text file as MARES output.   
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Density(): returns fDensity, the 2D density array. It stores fNe/(pi\*(pow(delta\_r,2) \+ 2\*r\*delta\_r)), where delta\_r is the radial segment size (standard 1mm).   
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> PlasmaFreq(): returns fPlasmaFrequency, the 2D plasma frequency matrix.   
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Absorption(): returns fAbsorption, a 2D array that stores the radio wave absorption at a specific point in the ionisation trail. std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> SkinDepth(): returns fSkinDepth, a 2D array containing the skindepth at a specific point in the ionisation trail.   
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Reflectance(): returns fReflectance, a 2D array containing the reflectance at each point in the ionisation trail.   
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Opacity(): returns fOpacity, a 2D array containing the opacity at each point in the ionisation trail.   
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Transparency(): returns fTransparency, a 2D array containing the transparency at each point in the ionisation trail. 


The constructor:   
Cascade has two constructors. The difference between them is the amount of input parameters that are given when creating a cascade object. In the end, the two constructors are strongly coupled as one calls the other with fixed values for some input parameters (see the cascade.cc file for clarification). In this document we describe the constructor with the most input parameters. The input parameters are: 

* xpos, ypos, and zpos of the cascade vertex in *m*.  
* zenith and azimuth angle of cascade direction in *deg*.  
* energy in *GeV*.  
* primaries: the number of primaries inducing the cascade ⇒ fNp.  
* n\_num: the primary identifier (dummy variable: not implemented yet)  
* t\_num: track id, to identify groups of neutrino events (dummy variable)  
* p\_id: particle id following PDG numbering, see [https://pdg.lbl.gov/2007/reviews/montecarlorpp.pdf](https://pdg.lbl.gov/2007/reviews/montecarlorpp.pdf) (dummy variable)   
* i\_type: the interaction type, e.g. CC (=0) or NC (=1) (dummy variable)   
* channel: subtype of interaction, e.b. hadronic \+ EM (dummy variable)   
* inelasticity: the Bjorken-y of the interaction ⇒ fBy (dummy variable)  
* oneweight: ⇒ fOneweight?


The above input parameters are used upon initialisation to assign values to the member variables: fEnergy, fNp, fPosition, fSphericalAngles, fParent, fBy, fOneweight. It also calculates the fDirection vector, fXtot, fLtot, fRtot. 

The member functions:

* void save\_output\_files(const std::string& output\_path, const std::array\<bool, 8\>& flags \= {0}): This function checks in the config file which 2D arrays (e.g. fNe,...) have to be saved. It uses the write\_2D\_array() function of settings.cc to do the actual writing to the text file saved at the output\_path location.    
* double Ne(double X, double Ep, double Np): This function calculates the number of ionised electrons per *cm* at a certain column depth X, for a certain primary energy Ep and Np number of primaries. It is assumed that all primaries have the same Ep and are co-located at the same point in space. Hence the Ne= Np\* NKG::N(X,Ep)\*  E\_deposition/E\_ionization \* rho\_ice. Where E\_deposition and E\_ionization can be set in the config file.   
* double Ne(double X): This function calls Ne(double X, double Ep, double Np) where it sets Ep=fEnergy and Np= fNp, the member variables of the class. This is a classic example of function overloading.   
* void Ne( const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&length\_vals, const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&radius\_vals, const double delta\_r): This function calculates the fNe 2D array. (not correctly implemented)  
* double Density(double X, double r, double delta\_r, double Ep, double Np): This function calculates the ionised electron density in *e\-/cm3* at a certain column depth X and lateral slice between r and r+delta\_r, for a certain primary energy Ep and Np number of primaries. It is assumed that all primaries have the same Ep and are co-located at the same point in space. Hence the density= Ne(X, Ep, Np)\*NKG::intwiv(r,delta\_r) / (pi\*(pow(delta\_r,2) \+ 2\*r\*delta\_r)). Where NKG::intwiv is the lateral parametrisation of the cascade.   
* double Density(double X, double r, double delta\_r): This function calls Density(double X, double r, double delta\_r, double Ep, double Np) where it sets Ep=fEnergy and Np= 1\.   
* void Density( const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&length\_vals,  const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&radius\_vals, const double delta\_r ): This functions calculates the 2D fDensity array. It loops over every segment in the (L,r) plane and uses Density(double X, double r, double delta\_r) for each point (note X= rho\_ice\*Li). Recall that fDensity corresponds with the electron density in the trail.   
* double PlasmaFreq(const double \&dens): This function returns the plasma frequency of the ionisation trail. This is “simply a measurement of the electron density in the frequency space” \- *Thesis* *Enrique Huesca Santiago*. The function returns: fp\= 8980 \* sqrt(memp) \* sqrt(dens\*pow(cm,3)))\*Hz, where memp is the effective plasma mass in electron masses (default set to 1\) and dens the considered local density in the ionisation trail.   
* void PlasmaFreq(const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&density): This function calculates the 2D fPlasmaFrequency array. It loops over all the points in the input density 2D array. This corresponds with the (L,r) plane of the cascade. Hence, the accessor is written such that when requesting fPlasmaFrequency, it uses the this function and inputs the fDensity array to calculate the corresponding plasma frequency (see double PlasmaFreq(const double \&dens) for the link between the two quantities).   
* double Absorption(const double \&dens, const double \&freq\_obs, const double \&freq\_nat \= 0): This function calculates and returns the absorption or attenuation due to the EM waves propagating through the ionisation trail. A clear explanation of how this ionisation trail attenuation is calculated, can be found in E. Huesca Santiago’s thesis in Chapter 9.2. The attenuation factor depends on the plasma frequency (that is calculated using the density, see PlasmaFreq() ), the natural frequency of the system (can be set to zero by good approximation) and the transmit frequency. It is equal to the imaginary part of the wavevector k: beta=sqrt((sqrt(pow(a,2) \+ pow(b,2)) \- a) /2 ), where a and b depend on the input parameters of the function (see code or thesis). This parameter has units *mm\-1*.   
* void Absorption(const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&density, const double & freq): This function calculates the 2D fAbsorption array. It loops over all the points in the input density 2D array which corresponds with the (L,r) plane of the cascade. It applies for every point Absorption(const double \&dens, const double \&freq\_obs, const double \&freq\_nat \= 0\) using the local density to find the local attenuation factor. Finally it saves it at the correct entry in the 2D fAbsorption array.   
* double SkinDepth(const double \&dens, const double \&freq\_obs, const double \&freq\_nat \= 0): This function calculates and returns the skindepth. It is defined as 1/Absorption(dens, freq\_obs, freq\_nat), and represents the length scale that an EM wave can travel through before reaching 1/e of its original electric field amplitude.   
* void SkinDepth(const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&density, const double & freq): This function calculates the 2D fSkinDepth array. It loops over all the points in the input density 2D array which corresponds with the (L,r) plane of the cascade. It applies for every point SkinDepth(const double \&dens, const double \&freq\_obs, const double \&freq\_nat \= 0\) using the local density to find the local skindepth. Finally it saves it at the correct entry in the 2D fSkinDepth array.   
* void Transparency(const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&density, const double & freq, const double & delta\_r): This function calculates three 2D arrays at once: fTransparency, fOpacity, fReflectance. These three quantities are strongly related and are expressing how the electric field amplitude changes due to the attenuation in the ionisation trail. The definitions can be found in the PhD thesis in Appendix A.2. fReflectance keeps track of the local attenuation when crossing a single segments in the r-direction with width delta\_r. fOpacity keeps track of the total amount of attenuation when crossing the ionisation trail from its edge to a certain depth in the r-direction. fTransparency is 1-fOpacity, the remaining electric field amplitude at a certain point in the ionisation trail. 


There are also two dedicated functions in the cascade.hh and cascade.cc. Note they are not member functions of the Cascade class. They are “helper functions” to make an instance of the Cascade class from a config file. 

* std::vector\<Cascade\> load\_cascade\_config(libconfig::Config& cs\_config, std::ostream& out \= std::cout): This function looks at the cascade list in your config file, creates a cascade object for each entry and adds it to a vector as an element. This vector consisting of all the cascade objects is returned by the function.   
* std::vector\<Cascade\> load\_cascade\_file(const std::string& cs\_config\_filepath, std::ostream& out \= std::cout): This function loads the cascades in MARES given the filepath to the config file and returns a vector with all Cascade objects. 

**NKG namespace**  
The strength of MARES is to use an analytical parametrisation for the induced particle cascade. This is described in the **namespace called NKG**. This namespace describes the analytical expression for the longitudinal and lateral part of the cascade and are combined together to get a 3D profile. The previous overloading functions such as Ne() and Density() use this namespace to find the ionised electron density profiles created by the energy deposition of the particle cascade in the ice. This namespace is not part of the Cascade class but is defined in the cascade.hh and cascade.cc files for obvious reasons. The namespace has four different member functions: 

* double N(double X, double E): This is the longitudinal parametrisation of the cascade given by the Greisen profile (see MARES paper eq 17: arXiv:2310.06731). Hence, this function returns the number of relativistic cascade particles at a column depth X for a primary energy E.   
* double ShowerAge(double X, double E): This is the parametrisation of the shower age. This quantity is typically used for air showers parametrisation. Its definition can be found in: [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.astropartphys.2014.05.009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.astropartphys.2014.05.009). The Greiser profile in N(double X, double E) depends on this quantity.  
* double wiv1(double r, double s): This function describes the lateral particle distribution of the cascade. It returns the number of particles at a radius r for a certain shower age s. Its definition can be found in the MARES paper  arXiv:2310.06731. Note that in the code an additional division by r\_moliere is performed. This is to normalise the profile (= Squeezing of the convergent distribution?)  
* double intwiv(double r, double delta\_r, double s \= 1.01, double imx \= 50.0): This function calculates the integral of lateral particle distribution between r and r \+ delta\_r. It uses a trapezoid integration method for this: [https://www.whitman.edu/mathematics/calculus\_online/section08.06.html](https://www.whitman.edu/mathematics/calculus_online/section08.06.html) . For in-ice particle cascades a s=1 can be assumed. Due to the divergences of the lateral distribution at s=1, by default s=1.01 in the MARES code. The number of integration steps between r and r/delta\_r is 50\. 


We can see that combining all the functions of the NKG namespace allows us to describe the entire particle cascade.  N(double X, double E) gives all the relativistic particles at a depth X. It thus assumes no lateral spread of the cascade and groups all particles at a fixed X into a single point. We can use the wiv1(double r, double s) to weight at each X how many particles are located at different lateral distances r. This how we get a full 3D parametrisation of the cascade. 

**Part 3: The scatter:**   
This part will cover how a complete radar echo scatter event is coded in MARES. It consists of a class called **Scatter** and a structure called **ScatterPoint.** The declaration and definition of the class and structure can be found in the scatter.hh, scatter.cc and scatter\_propagation.cc files. An important remark to make is the fact that this class uses *overloaded functions*. These functions have the same name but a different implementation, input variables and/or return type. These functions will be indicated in blue for extra clarity. 

1) **ScatterPoint structure**  
   A structure is a C++ construct to group a lot of related variables into one place. As the name suggests the ScatterPoint can be seen as a single point or segment inside the ionisation trail. MARES calculates the radar echo scatter from each segment in the trail. Below we list all the variables of a ScatterPoint object:   
* int ID: An identifier  
* double TCS: TCS \=  Th \* transparency \* damping \* N\_e^2  
* std::vector\<double\> Size{1,1,1}:   
* double L: Distance to the interaction vertex  
* std::vector\<double\> Position{0,0,0}: Position of the scatter point. The default is a zero-vector upon initialisation.  
* std::vector\<double\> TXDir{0, 0, 0}: Vector pointing from the transmitter to the scatter point. The default is a zero-vector upon initialisation.  
* std::vector\<double\> RXDir{0, 0, 0}: Vector pointing from the scatter point to the receiver. The default is a zero-vector upon initialisation.  
* double RTX:  Distance between TX and scatter point.  
* double RRX:  Distance between RX and scatter point.  
* double Phase: The phase of the scattered electric field originating from the point arriving at the receiver. This variable only takes into account the time independent part of the phase: k(R\_TX+R\_RX) \+ psi. (See MARES paper eq 20 for clarification).   
* double StartTime: This variable indicates when a scatter point is created after the vertex interaction took place. As the cascade develops in the ice with a speed c\_vac, the StarTime= L/c\_vac, where L is the distance of the scatter point to the vertex of the cascade.   
* double ArrivalTime: This variable indicates when the scattered electric field arrives for the first time at the receiver. This can be interpreted as the creation time of the segment from the point of view of the receiver. Depending on the chosen propagation mode, this quantity is calculated differently.   
* double Attenuation: This is the electric field attenuation due to propagation. Depending on which propagation mode is set, this attenuation factor is calculated differently.  
* std::vector\<double\> Polarization{0,0,0}: This is the polarisation of the electric field at the point, this is found assuming standard field equations (see MARES paper). Hence it is given by cross\_product(normalize(TXDir), cross\_product(normalize(TXDir), TX\_polarisation ) ).   
* std::vector\<double\> EFieldAtRX{0,0,0}: This is the direction of the electric field originating from the point at the receiver. Using the standard field equations this is given by cross\_product(normalize(RXDir),cross\_product(normalize(RXDir),Polarization) ).   
* double Directivity: This is the directivity of the scatter point since it acts as a secondary source. It is assumed and hardcoded that this scatter point acts as a hertzian dipole. Hence, Directivity=1.5\*norm(p.EFieldAtRX)(=1.5 sin²(theta), where theta is the opening angle between the polarisation of the point and the direction vector pointing to RX).   
* double PolEff: This is the polarisation efficiency and expresses the misalignment between the polarisation of the receiver antenna and scattered wave from the point. Hence it is given by PolEff \= abs(projection((EFieldAtRX), RX\_polarisation))).


The variables below are only relevant when running a scatter event with the IceRayTracing propagation mode. These save the output from iceraytracing in the corresponding variables to be used later on to work in the MARES code. Currently, IceRayTracing and MARES are not yet compatible. 

* double TXRayTime\[2\]:   
* double TXRayDistance\[2\]:  
* double TXRayStartAngle\[2\]:  
* double TXRayEndAngle\[2\]:  
* double TXRayAttenuation\[2\]:  
* double RXRayTime\[2\]:  
* double RXRayDistance\[2\]:  
* double RXRayStartAngle\[2\]:  
* double RXRayEndAngle\[2\]:  
* double RXRayAttenuation\[2\]:


2) **Scatter class**  
   This class allows to run a single scatter event for a bistatic antenna configuration. This implies there is one cascade, transmitter and receiver for which the radar echo is calculated.   
     
   The accessors:   
* Antenna TX(): returns fTX, the transmitter antenna.   
* Antenna RX(): returns fRX, the receiver antenna.   
* std::vector\<ScatterPoint\> Points(): returns fPoints, an array with all the scatter points of the trail.   
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Position(): returns the position of the scatter points. Note that there is no separate variable of the Scatter class saving this. Instead, it loops over all scatter points in fPoints and accesses the correct variable of the ScatterPoint structure, saves it element-wise in a vector and returns the latter when ending the loop.   
* std::vector\<double\> Phase(): returns the phase of all scatter points by looping over fPoints.   
* std::vector\<double\> ArrivalTime(): returns the arrival time of all scatter points by looping over fPoints.   
* std::vector\<double\> Attenuation(): returns the attenuation of all scatter points by looping over fPoints.  
* std::vector\<double\> Directivity(): returns the directivity of all scatter points by looping over fPoints.  
* std::vector\<double\> Polarization(): returns the polarisation of all scatter points by looping over fPoints.  
* std::vector\<double\> TCS(): returns the TCS of all scatter points by looping over fPoints.  
* std::vector\<double\> Duration(): returns fDuration, a vector containing the complete time trace of the scatter event.   
* std::vector\<double\> Voltage(): returns fVoltage, a vector containing the complete voltage trace of the scatter event.  
* std::vector\<double\> Power(): returns fPower, a vector containing the complete power trace of the scatter event.  
* std::vector\<double\> RCS(): returns fRCS, a vector containing the complete radar cross section (RCS) trace of the scatter event. This variable returns the total RCS of the trail over time, not that of an individual point in the trail.  
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Phase\_time(): returns fPhaseTime, a 2D array containing the phase value for each scatter point in the trail as a function of time. The rows correspond with time while the columns correspond with different scatter points.  
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> RCS\_time(): returns fRCSTime, a 2D array containing the RCS value for each scatter point in the trail as a function of time. The rows correspond with time while the columns correspond with different scatter points.  
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> E\_time(): returns fVoltageTime, a 2D array containing the observed voltage value at RX from each scatter point in the trail as a function of time. The rows correspond with time while the columns correspond with different scatter points.


  The constructor: 

  Scatter has two constructors. The difference between them is the amount of input parameters that are given when creating a Scatter object. In the end, the two constructors are strongly coupled as one calls the other with fixed values for some input parameters (see the scatter.cc file for clarification). In this document we describe the constructor with the most input parameters. The input parameters are: 

* Antenna& tx: the transmitter antenna  
* Antenna& rx: the receiver antenna  
* std::vector\<ScatterPoint\> points: the scatter points. These are determined by the particle cascade (so there is an indirect input of a cascade)  
* const double& sampling: this is the sampling ratio and is specified in the config file. MARES chooses as sampling rate the transmit\_frequency \* sampling (this input parameter). This ensures a satisfactory sampling for the waveform (Nyquist theorem). 


  The above input parameters are used upon initialisation to assign values to the member variables: fTX, fRX, fPoints, sampling\_ratio. The number of points is also saved as nP, that is by definition the size of the fPoints. Hence upon initialisation, this variable is set as well. The constructor can also be called without the scatter points input. In this case, the fPoints vector is taken empty upon initialisation. 


  The member functions:

* void UpdateRX(const Antenna& new\_RX): This function updates the receiver variable of the Scatter object to a new receiver given by the input new\_RX.  
* void AddPoint(const ScatterPoint& p): This function adds a new scatter point, p, to the fPoints vector of the Scatter class.   
* void AddPoints(const std::vector\<ScatterPoint\> new\_points): This function adds a vector of scatter points, new\_points, to the fPoints vector of the Scatter class.   
* void SetInDirection(std::vector\<double\> vertex,std::vector\<double\> direction,   double length, double rand\_seed \= 42): this functions places the ScatterPoints along a direction starting from a vertex position, equally spaced over a given length. To get rid of artifacts in the FFT, the positions can be given a small non-uniform randomisation along the direction of propagation. the input parameters are vertex (= the position of the vertex), the direction of the cascade, the length of the cascade, this will usually corresponds with fLtot of the Cascade object and a random seed.   
* void SetInPlane(std::vector\<double\> vertex, std::vector\<double\> l\_direction,std::vector\<double\> r\_direction, const std::vector\<double\> & l\_vals, const std::vector\<double\>& r\_vals): SetInPlane places the ScatterPoints in the lab frame  following an internal frame (the cascade frame usually) given by the directions of the frame and the positions within the frame {l\_vals, r\_vals}. (not used anywhere)  
* void RunScatter(const bool save2Dmatrices \= false): This function is the heart of running a scatter event. It is a time loop that calculates the observables at the receiver (fDuration, fVoltage, fPower,fRCS, fPhaseTime,fRCSTime, fVoltageTime). It computes the time integral of the interference of the scatter points at the receiver. Hence, it loops for every time step over all scatter points and calculates the electric field at the RX. As input parameter a boolean is given that indicates if the 2D arrays want to be saved. The run time is increased when this is set to True to the sometimes large size of the 2D array.   
*  void save\_output\_files(const std::string& output\_path, const std::array\<bool, 13\>& flags \= {0}): This function checks in the config file which outputs (e.g. fVoltage) have to be saved. It uses the write\_1D\_array() and write\_2D\_array() function of settings.cc to do the actual writing to the text file saved at the output\_path location.   
* void SetInConstIce(ScatterPoint& p): This function propagates the ray from a scatter point p to the receiver assuming straight lines. This corresponds with having an ice medium with a constant refractive index. Hence, it calculates the ScatterPoint variables TXDir, RTX, RXDir, RRx, ArrivalTime, Phase, Attenuation, Polarisation, EFieldAtRX,  Directivity and PolEff of the input point p.   
* void SetInConstIce(): This function runs void SetInConstIce(ScatterPoint& p) for all points in the fPoint array of Scatter. This implies straight rays are assumed in the simulation.   
* void SetWithIRT(ScatterPoint& p): This function propagates the ray from a scatter point p to the receiver using the [IceRayTracing software package](https://github.com/uzairlatif90/IceRayTracing/tree/master) (IRT). It calculates the necessary input parameters for IRT, runs the software and assigns the ScatterPoint variables TXDir, RTX, RXDir, RRx, ArrivalTime, Phase, Attenuation, Polarisation, EFieldAtRX,  Directivity and PolEff using the output from IRT.   
* void SetWithIRT():  This function runs void SetWithIRT(ScatterPoint& p) for all points in the fPoint array of Scatter. This implies realistic ray tracing is conducted for custom ice profiles.   
* void SetInBeam(ScatterPoint& p, const std::vector\<double\> interface\_plane,  const double& na, const double& nb):  This function is created for simulating a T-576-like setup. It handles the ray tracing from a scatter point p to the receiver for rays travelling through two, subsequent, media with refractive index *na* and *nb* separated by a certain interface. The *interface\_plane* argument is a vector containing the parameters of this plane defined by *Ax+By+Cz+D=0*.   
* void SetInBeam(const std::vector\<double\> plane, const double& na, const double& nb): This function runs void SetInBeam(ScatterPoint& p, const std::vector\<double\> interface\_plane,  const double& na, const double& nb) for all points in the fPoint array of Scatter. This mode allows for correct ray propagation when transitioning between two different media.   
* double estimate\_interface\_point( const double& ra, const double& rb, const double& lt, const double& n, const double& tolerance \= 1E-4, const int& n\_tries \= 1E4  ): This function estimates the point in the interface plane where the reflection happens. *ra* is the distance between the transmitter and the interface, *rb* is the distance between a scatter point p and the interface. *lt*  is the distance in the interface plane. Note that this function is only called within the SetInBeam(ScatterPoint p, …)  mode and nowhere else. Hence, it does not require a scatter point p as input variable. 

**Part 4: The one dimensional mode**   
This part will cover how MARES calculates the radar echo scatter assuming a one dimensional particle cascade. It starts from the classical two dimensional cascade described by its longitudinal and lateral development (L,r) and reduces it to a pure longitudinal cascade. This is a valid assumption in most cases as the lateral size of the cascade is approximately two orders of magnitude smaller than the longitudinal. The class **Cascade1D** is designed to perform this calculation. It is a derived class *(inheritance)* from the two base classes Scatter and Cascade, described above. This implies that a Cascade1D object *knows* all member functions and variables of these two classes. It is noted here that this class defines three different reference frames for performing different calculations. The figure below is found in Enrique Huesca Santiago’s PhD thesis and supports the explanation of the three frames. A complete in-depth outline can be found in his thesis (**add ref to thesis)**.   
 

1. The lab frame: (shown in orange) This reference frame has as origin the TX antenna and e\_x direction pointed from the TX to the RX, hence the baseline. The e\_z component is the local Earth Vertical. This frame is the natural radar frame that allows defining the cascade by the position of the interaction vertex R\_T and its momentum vector p\_CS.   
     
2. The cascade frame: (shown in red) This is the *natural* frame of the cascade. It has as its origin the interaction vertex and is defined by the momentum vector of the cascade and the plane perpendicular to this vector. The electron density is parametrised in this frame by the NKG parametrisation.   
     
3. The line of sight (LOS) frame or TX frame: (shown in blue) This frame uses as origin the interaction vertex of the cascade. Three basis vectors are given by ![][image1]  
   Thanks to e\_b being the basis vector that corresponds with the LOS wrt to the lab frame, this reference frame is ideal for calculating the transparency of the cascade when radio waves propagate through and lose power.

![][image2]  
The accessors:

* std::vector\<double\> TCS(): returns fTCS, a vector containing the transparency value for each scatter point in the fPoints vector of the Scatter class.  
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Radius(): returns fCSRadius, a 2D matrix that contains the radius values of the cascade in the transmitter frame  
* std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> Length(): returns fCSLength, a 2D matrix that contains the length values of the cascade in the transmitter frame

The constructor:   
This class has a single constructor. It requires as input the transmitter, receiver and cascade objects, the dimensions of the segments in the cascade frame *dL* and *dR* and the sampling rate. These inputs are used to make a Scatter object (using tx,rx and sampling rate) and a Cascade object. The distances between the scatterpoints and the transmitter and receiver are immediately calculated (using SetDirection()) and assigned as well as the opening angles (using SetAngle()). 

The member functions: 

* void SetTXFrame(): This function calculates the electron density matrix (fDensity) and electron number matrix (fNe). Note that there exist separate functions for this outlined before. These are always for calculating this matrix in the cascade frame while in the Cascade1D we need it in the TX frame?  
* void SetInCSPlane(std::vector\<double\> vertex, std::vector\<double\> direction,                    std::vector\<double\> & l\_vals, const std::vector\<double\>& r\_vals): Not used anywhere \+ unclear what its purpose is  
* void SetInMax(std::vector\<double\> vertex, std::vector\<double\> direction, const double& dL, const double& dR, const std::vector\<std::vector\<double\>\> \&variable): This function determines finds the points of largest value for fixed L in the 2D matrix *variable* and centers the scatter points at these locations. Not used anywhere  
* void SetInMaxReflectivty(): This function first calculates the fReflectance 2D matrix, after which it passes this matrix to the void SetInMax() function. This implies that the centers of the scatter points are set to    
* void SetTCS(): This function calculates the transparency of each Scatterpoint. Note that here the conversion to a 1D problem becomes clear as the cumulative effect of the ray propagating through the radial segments is calculated. After looping over the full 2D density matrix, the transparency of the 1D longitudinal profile is saved in the fTCS vector.   
* void SetInDirection(double rand\_seed \= 42): This function calls the void SetInDirection() function from the scatter class with fixed random\_seed=42. See the Scatter class for more information.  
* void UpdateRX(const Antenna& new\_RX): This function allows for updating the RX antenna. This is a function that allows MARES to efficiently run, not needing to resegment the cascade for every TX-CS-RX combo as the segmentation only depends on the CS and its orientation w.r.t. the TX. 

**Part 5: Predefined functions, settings and constants in MARES**  
This part covers the content in the *settings\_units\_constants.hh, settings.hh, settings\_math.cc, settings.cc* files. They contain the information about the units used in the MARES code, self-defined functions for mathematical calculations and writing the output in text-files and loading and reading a config file using libconfig. 

**Part 6: The MARES executable**  
This part covers the MARES executable, the script that is run to perform a MARES simulation. It simply loads and reads the config file, sets all the parameters correctly, loads the antennas and cascades, runs the simulations for all TX-CS-RX combos and writes the output in the text-files. All of this is done using the Classes and their member functions described above
